content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 243M of the Constitution of India is titled “Part not to apply to certain areas”. It forms an integral component of The Panchayats (Articles 243–243O), located within the “Panchayats” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) Nothing in this Part shall apply to the Scheduled Areas referred to in clause (1), and the tribal areas referred to in clause (2), of article 244.

(2) Nothing in this Part shall apply to—

(a) the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram;

(b) the hill areas in the State of Manipur for which District Councils exist under any law for the time being in force.

(3) Nothing in this Part—

(a) relating to Panchayats at the district level shall apply to the hill areas of the District of Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal for which Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council exists under any law for the time being in force;

(b) shall be construed to affect the functions and powers of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council constituted under such law. (3A) Nothing in article 243D, relating to reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes, shall apply to the State of Arunachal Pradesh.

(4) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,—

(a) the Legislature of a State referred to in sub-clause ( a) of clause (2) may, by law, extend this Part to that State, except the areas, if any, referred to in clause (1), if the Legislative Assembly of that State passes a resolution to that effect by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting;

(b) Parliament may, by law, extend the provisions of this Part to the Scheduled Areas and the tribal areas referred to in clause (1) subject to such exceptions and modifications as may be specified in such law, and no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 243M as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. It regulates executive, legislative, or fundamental citizen interests to maintain the rule of law and constitutional supremacy.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) Nothing in this Part shall apply to the Scheduled Areas referred to in clause (1), and the tribal areas referred to in clause (2), of article 244.
2. (2) Nothing in this Part shall apply to—
3. (a) the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram;
4. (b) the hill areas in the State of Manipur for which District Councils exist under any law for the time being in force.
5. (3) Nothing in this Part—
6. (a) relating to Panchayats at the district level shall apply to the hill areas of the District of Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal for which Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council exists under any law for the time being in force;

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 243M is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

Article-specific doctrinal analysis and application
Article 243M limits the ordinary application of Part IX through territorial and institutional exclusions and qualifications, including arrangements connected with Scheduled Areas and tribal areas under Article 244 and specified northeastern and hill-area contexts. Parliament may extend Part IX to certain excluded areas with modifications under the constitutional mechanism. Do not infer applicability merely from the existence of a village council: classify the territory, consult the current article text and any extension legislation, and identify the governing state or customary framework.

1. Scrutinize the constitutional source of power: Does Article 243M grant plenary power, or is it conditioned by express safeguards, legislative competence, or fundamental rights?

questionsAndAnswers.question: Case Brief & Legal Assessment: Scope and Application of Article 243M (Part not to apply to certain areas)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 243M (Part not to apply to certain areas) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 243M is situated in The Panchayats (Articles 243–243O), governing the “Panchayats” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) Nothing in this Part shall apply to the Scheduled Areas referred to in clause (1), and the tribal areas referred to in clause (2), of article 244.
2. (2) Nothing in this Part shall apply to—
3. (a) the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram;
4. (b) the hill areas in the State of Manipur for which District Councils exist under any law for the time being in force.
5. (3) Nothing in this Part—
6. (a) relating to Panchayats at the district level shall apply to the hill areas of the District of Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal for which Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council exists under any law for the time being in force;

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225, the Supreme Court established that The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 243M:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 243M stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 243M of the Constitution of India, titled “Part not to apply to certain areas”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The Panchayats (Articles 243–243O), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 243M reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) Nothing in this Part shall apply to the Scheduled Areas referred to in clause (1), and the tribal areas referred to in clause (2), of article 244.
(a) Limb 2: (2) Nothing in this Part shall apply to—
(a) Limb 3: (a) the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram;
(a) Limb 4: (b) the hill areas in the State of Manipur for which District Councils exist under any law for the time being in force.
(a) Limb 5: (3) Nothing in this Part—
(a) Limb 6: (a) relating to Panchayats at the district level shall apply to the hill areas of the District of Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal for which Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council exists under any law for the time being in force;
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 243M must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 243M across several seminal judgments:
1. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) (1973) 4 SCC 225:
   Ratio Decidendi: The Constitution is the supreme law of the land; constitutional provisions must be harmoniously construed to preserve its basic structure and core institutional balance.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 243M:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 243M;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 243M without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 243M?
Rule: Under Article 243M, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 243M remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

ARTICLE 243M (Part not to apply to certain areas) is an essential structural provision in Part IX: The Panchayats of the Constitution of India.

### Constitutional Text & Clauses
(1) Nothing in this Part shall apply to the Scheduled Areas referred to in clause (1), and the tribal areas referred to in clause (2), of article 244.

(2) Nothing in this Part shall apply to—

(a) the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram;

(b) the hill areas in the State of Manipur for which District Councils exist under any law for the time being in force.

(3) Nothing in this Part—

(a) relating to Panchayats at the district level shall apply to the hill areas of the District of Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal for which Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council exists under any law for the time being in force;

(b) shall be construed to affect the functions and powers of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council constituted under such law. (3A) Nothing in article 243D, relating to reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes, shall apply to the State of Arunachal Pradesh.

(4) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,—

(a) the Legislature of a State referred to in sub-clause ( a) of clause (2) may, by law, extend this Part to that State, except the areas, if any, referred to in clause (1), if the Legislative Assembly of that State passes a resolution to that effect by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting;

(b) Parliament may, by law, extend the provisions of this Part to the Scheduled Areas and the tribal areas referred to in clause (1) subject to such exceptions and modifications as may be specified in such law, and no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.

### Constituent Intent & Doctrinal Evolution
The framers envisioned Article 243M as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. It regulates executive, legislative, or fundamental citizen interests to maintain the rule of law and constitutional supremacy.

### Operational Mechanics & Judicial Standards
In practice, ARTICLE 243M functions as a direct constitutional parameter binding executive and legislative action. The Supreme Court of India has consistently held that powers exercised under this provision are not unfettered; they must comply with the overarching constitutional discipline of the Rule of Law, Article 14 non-arbitrariness, and the basic features of the Constitution. Aggrieved parties may invoke the writ jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226 or the Supreme Court under Article 32 to challenge actions that transgress the constitutional boundaries of this article.
examples: Factual scenario (Constitutional Compliance): An authority acts strictly within the procedural and substantive bounds of ARTICLE 243M, issuing a reasoned order after satisfying all conditions precedent. On judicial review, the High Court upholds the measure, confirming that the exercise of power conforms to Part IX: The Panchayats and constitutional safeguards.

Factual scenario (Ultra Vires Action): An authority bypasses the mandatory statutory prerequisites under ARTICLE 243M, acting arbitrarily or in excess of constitutional competence. The Supreme Court intervenes, holding that constitutional limitations cannot be sacrificed for administrative expediency, and quashes the impugned action.
distinctions: ARTICLE 243M vs General Administrative Power: Powers exercised under ARTICLE 243M derive directly from the Constitution and enjoy supremacy over ordinary statutes and subordinate rules.

ARTICLE 243M vs Fundamental Rights in Part III: Any measure enacted or executed under ARTICLE 243M remains subordinate to the Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19, and 21 unless expressly protected by a saving clause.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an order passed in purported exercise of power under ARTICLE 243M without fulfilling statutory conditions precedent is constitutionally valid.
Rule: Exercise of constitutional authority under ARTICLE 243M requires strict adherence to mandatory procedural and substantive conditions precedent.
Application: The record reveals that the authority acted without recording requisite satisfaction and bypassed procedural safeguards mandated by Part IX: The Panchayats.
Counterargument: The State asserts broad executive discretion and administrative necessity.
Conclusion: The impugned order is ultra vires ARTICLE 243M and void for manifest arbitrariness under Article 14.
